modelAnswer: The primary objectives of computer networks are resource sharing, data communication and collaboration.
Resource sharing: Computer networks allow devices to share resources, such as printers and storage, reducing costs and improving efficiency.

Data communication: Networks facilitate data transfer, enabling communication through emails, instant messaging, and video conferencing.
Example: Employees in different locations can collaborate through video conferencing tools like Zoom or Microsoft Teams.
Connectivity and collaboration: Networks connect devices, allowing for remote access and collaboration, improving productivity and flexibility.
Example: A team can work on a shared document in real-time using cloud-based services like Google Drive.

writtenQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the different types of network topologies (star, ring, bus, and mesh).
modelAnswer: In a bus topology, all devices share a single communication line called a bus.
If the main cable fails, the whole network goes down.
In a star topology, each node communicates with the others via a central switch or hub.
The hub works as a data flow repeater.
In a ring topology, each device is connected in a circular pathway with other devices.
Data travels in one direction, passing through each device; if one connection fails, the whole network is affected.
In a mesh topology, each device is connected to every other device.
This provides high redundancy and reliability because data can be rerouted through other links.

explain.title: The OSI model has seven layers
explain.body: The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) Model is a framework used to understand how different networking protocols interact. It has 7 layers, each with a specific function. From bottom to top, the layers are Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application.

explain.title: Physical and Data Link layers
explain.body: The Physical Layer is liable for the actual connection between devices. The process of sending unprocessed data bits via a physical medium is the focus here. The Data Link Layer handles error detection and correction, as well as node-to-node data transport. It ensures error-free data transmission from the Physical Layer.

explain.title: Network and Transport layers
explain.body: The Network Layer is responsible for data transfer between different networks. It determines the best path for data to travel from the source to the destination. The Transport Layer ensures that data is transferred from one process rerunning on source end system to a process souring on destination end system. It manages data flow control and error checking.

explain.title: Session and Presentation layers
explain.body: The Session Layer manages sessions between applications. It establishes, maintains, and terminates connections between devices. The Presentation Layer translates data between the application layer and the network. It formats and encrypts data to ensure it is readable by the receiving system.

explain.title: Application layer
explain.body: The Application Layer is the closest to the end user. It provides network services directly to applications, such as email, web browsing, and file transfer.

Do not describe UDP as guaranteeing reliable delivery; TCP is the reliable protocol in this comparison.
For transmission time, do not divide kilobytes directly by a rate in bits per second; convert to bits first.
In a shift cipher, use opposite directions for encryption and decryption and apply the same shift amount.
Do not confuse 10% reserved with 10% remaining; the remaining share is 90%.

notes.title: Network as a System
notes.answer: A computer network is a system of linked devices and computers that may exchange data and operate together.
notes.explanation: A computer network links devices so they can exchange data and work together. Nodes are the connected devices, and links connect those nodes. Switches forward data within a network; routers connect different networks. Networks help people share resources, communicate, and collaborate.
notes.simple: A network is a group of connected devices that can share information and resources.
examples: Several office computers share one printer.
Employees at different locations meet through video conferencing.
steps: Identify the nodes: these are devices connected to the network.
Identify the links: these connect the nodes, either by wire or wirelessly.
Use switches to forward data within a network.
Use routers to connect different networks and direct data packets.
notes.checkQuestion: What does a switch do in a network?
notes.checkAnswer: A switch forwards data between nodes within a network.

notes.title: The five components of data communication
notes.answer: The five components are sender, receiver, message, protocol, and medium.
notes.explanation: Data communication is the exchange of data between a sender and a receiver through a medium. The five components tell us who sends the data, who receives it, what is sent, which rules are followed, and how the data travels.
notes.simple: Data communication means sending data from one device to another. Remember the five parts: sender, receiver, message, protocol, and medium.
examples: A computer sends an email: the computer is the sender, the smartphone is the receiver, and the email content is the message.
The data may travel through an Ethernet cable or Wi-Fi; these are examples of a medium.
steps: Identify the device that sends the data: the sender.
Identify the device that receives the data: the receiver.
Identify the data being sent: the message.
Identify the rules for communicating: the protocol.
Identify the path the data travels through: the medium.
notes.checkQuestion: Which component is the set of rules governing data communication?

notes.title: Networking Devices
notes.answer: Switches connect and direct data between devices within a network; routers direct packets between networks; access points connect wireless devices to a wired network.
notes.explanation: A switch connects devices within a network and uses MAC addresses to send data to the intended device. A router connects different networks and directs data packets between them. An access point connects wireless devices to a wired network.
notes.simple: A switch directs data inside a network, a router directs data between networks, and an access point links wireless devices to a wired network.
examples: A switch sends a packet to the computer whose MAC address matches the packet’s destination address.
A router directs packets between a home network and another network.
steps: Identify whether the data is moving within one network or between networks.
For devices communicating within a network, a switch uses destination MAC addresses to forward data.
For data moving between networks, a router finds a path and directs the packets.
For wireless devices joining a wired network, an access point receives and transmits data wirelessly.
notes.checkQuestion: What does a router do with data packets?
notes.checkAnswer: A router directs data packets between different networks.

notes.title: Network Topologies
notes.answer: A network topology is the arrangement of devices in a network.
notes.explanation: A network topology describes how devices (nodes) are arranged and connected. The main types in this section are bus, star, ring, and mesh.
notes.simple: Topology is the shape or pattern of the connections between devices in a network.
examples: In a star topology, a central switch or hub connects to the other devices.
In a mesh topology, every device connects to every other device.
steps: Identify how the devices are connected.
Match that arrangement to bus, star, ring, or mesh.
Remember the important feature or weakness of that topology.
notes.checkQuestion: Which topology connects each device to every other device?

notes.title: Choosing a Transmission Mode
notes.answer: Simplex sends in one direction only; Half-Duplex allows both directions one at a time; Full-Duplex allows both directions simultaneously.
notes.explanation: Transmission modes describe the direction and timing of data flow between devices. Simplex is one-way, Half-Duplex is two-way but takes turns, and Full-Duplex is two-way at the same time.
notes.simple: Ask two questions: Can data go both ways? Can it go both ways at the same time?
steps: Check whether data travels in one direction or both directions.
If it travels in one direction only, the mode is Simplex.
If it travels in both directions but the devices take turns, the mode is Half-Duplex.
If both devices can send and receive at the same time, the mode is Full-Duplex.
notes.checkQuestion: Two people use walkie-talkies and take turns speaking. Which transmission mode is this?

notes.title: What does the Network Layer do?
notes.answer: The Network Layer transfers data between different networks and determines the best path for data to travel from source to destination.
notes.explanation: The Network Layer transfers data between different networks and selects a path from source to destination. For example, it is like a GPS choosing a route from home to school. The Data Link Layer handles node-to-node transfer, while the Network Layer handles transfer between networks.
notes.simple: The Network Layer is like a GPS for data: it helps data travel between networks by choosing a path.
examples: A GPS finding a route is an example of the Network Layer choosing a path.
IP addresses help the Network Layer route data between networks.
steps: Identify the source and destination networks.
Use IP addresses to route the data.
Determine the best path from source to destination.
notes.checkQuestion: Which OSI layer determines the best path for data to travel between networks?
notes.checkAnswer: The Network Layer transfers data between different networks and determines the best path from source to destination.

notes.title: IPv4 and IPv6 address sizes
notes.answer: IPv4 uses 32 bits; IPv6 uses 128 bits.
notes.explanation: IPv4 uses 32 bits, so it has 2³² = 4,294,967,296 possible addresses. IPv6 uses 128 bits and was designed to provide many more addresses as the number of internet-connected devices grew. The textbook’s IPv4 example, 172.16.254.1, has four decimal parts, each corresponding to an 8-bit binary group.
notes.simple: IPv4 is like a set of 4.3 billion address labels. IPv6 uses far more bits, so it can provide vastly more labels for connected devices.
examples: IPv4: 172.16.254.1 has four 8-bit groups.
IPv6: 2001:0000:130F:0000:0000:0900:876A:130B is an example of an IPv6 address.
steps: Count the bits in an IPv4 address: 32.
Calculate its possible addresses: 2³² = 4,294,967,296.
An IPv4 address is written as four decimal numbers, each from 0 to 255.
Count the bits in an IPv6 address: 128.
Remember that IPv6 was designed to address the depletion of IPv4 addresses.
notes.checkQuestion: How many bits does an IPv6 address use?

notes.title: Protocols, DNS and DHCP
notes.answer: Protocols are sets of rules that govern data communication. DNS translates domain names to IP addresses, and DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses to devices on a network.
notes.explanation: Protocols are rules for communication between devices. DNS looks up the IP address for a domain name, while DHCP automatically gives an IP address to a device on a network.
notes.simple: DNS finds the address of a website. DHCP gives a connected device its network address.
examples: Typing www.example.com in a browser: DNS translates the domain name to its IP address.
Connecting a device to Wi-Fi: DHCP assigns the device an IP address.
steps: Identify what the device or user needs.
Use DNS to translate a domain name to an IP address.
Use DHCP to assign an IP address automatically when a device connects to a network.
notes.checkQuestion: Which protocol automatically assigns IP addresses to devices on a network?
notes.checkAnswer: DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses to devices on a network.

notes.title: Network Security
notes.answer: Network security uses measures such as firewalls, encryption, and authentication to protect data and prevent unauthorized access to networks.
notes.explanation: Network security protects data and networks from unauthorized access and attacks. Firewalls monitor and control network traffic, encryption makes data unreadable without the correct decryption key, and passwords and authentication help ensure that only authorized users can access network resources.
notes.simple: Network security is like protecting a house: a firewall is the gatekeeper, encryption is a secret code, and a password helps check who is allowed in.
examples: A firewall can block unwanted network traffic.
A shift cipher changes “Hello” to “Khoor” by moving each letter three places down the alphabet.
steps: Use a firewall to monitor and control incoming and outgoing network traffic.
Encrypt sensitive data so that only someone with the correct decryption key can understand it.
Use passwords and authentication to check that users are authorized.
Watch for threats such as malware, phishing, DoS attacks, and man-in-the-middle attacks.
notes.checkAnswer: A firewall monitors and controls network traffic according to security rules.

notes.title: Choosing a network type by its coverage
notes.answer: A CAN connects multiple LANs within a limited geographical area, such as a university campus.
notes.explanation: Choose the network type by looking at the size and area it covers. A few personal devices nearby use a PAN; devices in one home, school, or office use a LAN; multiple LANs across a campus use a CAN or across a city use a MAN; a very large geographical area uses a WAN.
notes.simple: Think about how far the network reaches: personal devices, one local place, a campus, a city, or a very large area.
examples: A smartphone connected to a wireless headset by Bluetooth forms a PAN.
A network connecting different branch offices of a company across countries is a WAN.
steps: Identify the area covered by the network.
Check whether it connects personal devices, one limited area, a campus, a city, or a large geographical area.
Match that area to PAN, LAN, CAN, MAN, or WAN.
notes.checkQuestion: What type of network connects several LANs within a university campus?

notes.title: Real-World Applications of Computer Networks
notes.answer: Businesses use intranets to share information and resources securely; educational institutions use networks for online learning and educational resources; healthcare networks support sharing patient information, telemedicine, and access to medical databases.
notes.explanation: Computer networks are useful in business, education, and healthcare. They help people communicate, share resources, and manage information.
notes.simple: Networks connect people and information. Businesses use them to work together, schools use them for learning, and hospitals use them to manage patient information.
examples: Companies use intranets to share information and resources securely within the organization.
Hospitals use Electronic Health Records (EHR) systems to store and retrieve patient data efficiently.
steps: Identify the setting: business, education, or healthcare.
State what the network helps people do in that setting.
Give a relevant example, such as an intranet, LMS, or EHR system.
notes.checkQuestion: Name one network application in each of business, education, and healthcare.
notes.checkAnswer: Networks are used in business to communicate and share resources, in education to provide online learning and educational resources, and in healthcare to share patient information and access medical databases.

notes.title: Standard Protocols in TCP/IP Communications
notes.answer: DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses; DNS translates domain names to IP addresses.
notes.explanation: TCP/IP is the main suite of protocols used for internet communication. TCP provides reliable data transfer, while IP handles addressing and routing. DNS translates domain names into IP addresses, and DHCP automatically assigns IP addresses.
notes.simple: Think of these protocols as different helpers: TCP checks that data transfers reliably, IP handles packet addresses and routes, DNS looks up IP addresses from domain names, and DHCP assigns IP addresses automatically.
examples: When a device needs an IP address automatically, DHCP performs that task.
When a domain name needs to be translated into an IP address, DNS performs that task.
steps: Identify the task: reliable transfer, addressing and routing, faster transfer, name translation, or automatic IP assignment.
Match the task to the protocol: TCP, IP, UDP, DNS, or DHCP, respectively.
notes.checkQuestion: Which protocol automatically assigns IP addresses, and which protocol translates domain names to IP addresses?
notes.checkAnswer: TCP provides reliable data transfer; UDP provides faster, but less reliable, data transfer.

notes.title: Network security methods
notes.answer: Firewalls, encryption, and antivirus software work together to provide robust network security.
notes.explanation: Network security protects data and helps prevent unauthorized access. Your textbook describes three methods: firewalls monitor and control network traffic, encryption converts data into a secure format, and antivirus software detects and removes malicious software.
notes.simple: A firewall checks network traffic, encryption scrambles data into a secure format, and antivirus software finds and removes harmful software.
steps: Firewall: Monitor and control incoming and outgoing network traffic.
Encryption: Protects data by converting it into a secure format.
Antivirus software: Detects and removes malicious software.
Example: A combination of firewalls, encryption, and antivirus software provides robust network security.
notes.checkQuestion: What does encryption do to data?
notes.checkAnswer: Encryption converts data into a secure format.

written.text: Q6.3. Describe how data is transmitted across computer networks using packet switching and circuit switching.

At the destination, the packets are put back together to form the original message.
In circuit switching, a dedicated communication path is established before data is sent.
The path remains reserved for the communication while it is in use.
Packet switching shares network capacity among packets, while circuit switching reserves a path.
Thus, the two methods differ in whether data uses shared routes or a dedicated connection.

written.text: Q6.7. Compare and contrast the different types of network topologies (star, ring, bus, and mesh).
modelAnswer: In a star topology, each device connects to a central hub or switch.
It is easy to manage, and one device or link failing usually does not stop the other devices, but the central device is a critical point.
In a ring topology, each device connects to two neighbouring devices to form a closed loop.
A break in the ring can disrupt communication unless a bypass or other protection is available.
In a bus topology, all devices share one main backbone cable.
It uses less cable, but a failure of the backbone can affect the whole network and faults may be harder to locate.
In a mesh topology, devices have multiple links or paths between them.
Mesh can be highly reliable because data may use another path, but it can require more connections and cost more.
Therefore, the topologies differ in arrangement, cost, reliability, and ease of maintenance.
